---
title: "When Does an Intent Attribution Earn Its Keep?"
description: "Intent attributions are useful when they distinguish competing explanations through falsifiable predictions."
date: "2026-10-09"
categories: [evaluation, AI safety]
draft: false
toc: false
---

The same concerning behavior can imply very different risks. A model might bypass a constraint because doing so helps it complete the current task, because it has learned a broader habit of disregarding restrictions, or because the action serves a persistent objective that conflicts with ours. Those explanations matter only if they lead to different predictions.

For example, suppose a model circumvents a network restriction. If a local incentive to finish the task drives the behavior, removing that incentive should reduce circumvention. If avoiding oversight is itself part of a persistent objective, blocking one route may simply push the model toward another.

But even that comparison is not enough. A model motivated only by task completion might also search for another route.

Two comparisons would provide stronger evidence:

- **Remove the task advantage.** Provide an authorized route that the model recognizes as equally effective. If the model still prefers the route that reduces oversight, that is better evidence for the oversight-related hypothesis.
- **Vary the oversight consequence.** Hold task benefit fixed and vary whether circumvention reduces oversight. If behavior tracks opportunities to reduce oversight, it supports the hypothesis. If it tracks only task-completion advantages, it weakens the hypothesis.

The controls matter. An “equally effective” route may not look equally reliable to the model, and changing oversight cues may change how it interprets the task. A useful test therefore needs evidence that the model understands the alternatives and their consequences.

Persistence also needs a scope. Behavior recurring within one conversation, across tasks with shared memory, and across fresh sessions supports progressively broader claims. “Persistent objective” should not become a label that outruns the evidence.

However, none of this makes understanding intent a prerequisite for acting. Restricting network access, reducing permissions, and requiring human approval can buy safety while the diagnosis remains uncertain. Several explanations can justify these mitigations.

The crux is whether an intent attribution makes falsifiable predictions.

Saying a model “has a persistent objective to avoid oversight” adds little if that merely redescribes the fact that it broke a rule. The attribution earns its keep when it predicts behavior under interventions that plausible alternatives do not.
